nodes.name: h-principle (informal)
nodes.statement: He says that a geometric construction problem satisfies the $h$-principle if the only obstructions to the existence of a solution come from algebraic topology.
differentia: the only obstructions to the existence of a solution come from algebraic topology

nodes.name: flexible and rigid construction
nodes.statement: In this case, the construction is called flexible, otherwise it is called rigid.

nodes.name: homotopy of immersions
nodes.statement: The geometric object we want to construct is a (smooth) homotopy of immersions from $f_0$ to $f_1$, ie a smooth map $F \co 𝕊^1 × [0, 1] → ℝ^2$ such that $\rst{F}{𝕊^1 × \{0\}} = f_0$, $\rst{F}{𝕊^1 × \{1\}} = f_1$, and each $f_p := \rst{F}{𝕊^1 × \{p\}}$ is an immersion.
nodes.statement_short: A homotopy of immersions from $f_0$ to $f_1$ is a smooth map $F$ on $𝕊^1×[0,1]$ restricting to $f_0,f_1$ with each slice an immersion.

nodes.name: winding number
nodes.statement: Such maps have a well defined winding number $w(f'_i) ∈ ℤ$ around the origin, the degree of the normalized map $f'_i/‖f'_i‖ \co 𝕊^1 → 𝕊^1$.

nodes.name: Whitney–Graustein theorem
nodes.statement: So $w(f_0') = w(f_1')$ is a necessary condition for the existence of $F$, which comes from algebraic topology. The Whitney--Graustein theorem states that this necessary condition is also sufficient.
nodes.statement_short: Two immersions of the circle in the plane are homotopic through immersions iff their derivatives have the same winding number.
conclusions: this necessary condition is also sufficient

nodes.name: Hopf degree theorem (one-dimensional)
nodes.statement: Indeed the (one-dimensional) Hopf degree theorem ensures that, provided $w(f'_0) = w(f'_1)$, there exists a homotopy $g_p$ of nowhere vanishing maps relating $f'_0$ and $f'_1$.
assumptions: provided $w(f'_0) = w(f'_1)$
conclusions: there exists a homotopy $g_p$ of nowhere vanishing maps relating $f'_0$ and $f'_1$

nodes.name: Whitney–Graustein theorem (second form)
nodes.statement: So we can restate the crucial part of the Whitney--Graustein theorem as: there is a homotopy of immersion from $f_0$ to $f_1$ as soon as there is (a homotopy from $f_0$ to $f_1$) and a homotopy from $f_0'$ to $f_1'$ among nowhere vanishing maps.
nodes.statement_short: A homotopy of immersions exists as soon as there is a homotopy of maps and a homotopy of derivatives among nowhere vanishing maps.
assumptions: there is (a homotopy from $f_0$ to $f_1$) and a homotopy from $f_0'$ to $f_1'$ among nowhere vanishing maps
conclusions: there is a homotopy of immersion from $f_0$ to $f_1$

nodes.name: formal solution (informal)
nodes.statement: Gromov says that such a homotopy of uncoupled pairs $(f, g)$ is a formal solution of the original problem.

nodes.name: 1-jet space
nodes.statement: The so called $1$-jet space $J^1(M, N)$ is the space of triples $(m, n, φ)$ with $m ∈ M$, $n ∈ N$, and $φ ∈ \Hom(T_mM, T_nN)$, the space of linear maps from $T_mM$ to $T_nN$.

nodes.name: first order differential relation, solution, formal solution and h-principle (introduction)
nodes.statement: A first order differential relation $\Rel$ for maps from $M$ to $N$ is a subset of $J^1(M, N)$. A solution of $\Rel$ is a function $f \co M \to N$ such that $j^1f(m)$ is in $\Rel$ for all $m$. A \emph{formal solution} of $\Rel$ is a non-necessarily holonomic section of $J^1(M, N) → M$ which takes value in $\Rel$. The partial differential relation $\Rel$ satisfies the $h$-principle if any formal solution $σ$ of $\Rel$ is homotopic, among formal solutions, to some holonomic one $j^1f$.
nodes.statement_short: A relation is a subset of $J^1(M,N)$; solutions have 1-jet in it; formal solutions are sections in it; the h-principle says formal solutions deform to holonomic ones.

nodes.name: immersion relation
nodes.statement: For instance, an immersion of $M$ into $N$ is a solution of \[ \Rel = \{(m, n, φ) ∈ J^1(M, N) \;|\; φ \text{ is injective}\}. \]
nodes.statement_short: The immersion relation: 1-jets $(m,n,φ)$ with $φ$ injective.

nodes.name: smooth family of maps
nodes.statement: In differential topology, a smooth family of maps between manifolds $X$ and $Y$ is a smooth map $h \co P × X → Y$ seen as the collection of maps $h_p \co x ↦ h(p, x)$.

nodes.name: smooth family of sections
nodes.statement: A smooth family of sections of $E → X$ is a smooth family of maps $σ \co P × X → E$ such that each $σ_p$ is a section.

nodes.name: relative and parametric h-principle
nodes.statement: A partial differential relation $\Rel ⊂ J^1(M, N)$ satisfies the relative and parametric $h$-principle if every family of formal solutions $σ \co M × P → J^1(M, N)$ which are holonomic for $(p, m)$ near some closed set $C ⊂ P × M$, is homotopic to a family of holonomic sections, and this homotopy can be chosen constant near $C$.
nodes.statement_short: Families of formal solutions holonomic near a closed set $C$ deform to holonomic families, rel. $C$.

nodes.name: C^0-dense h-principle
nodes.statement: One can also insist on the deformed solution to be $C^0$-close to the original one. In this case one talks about a $C^0$-dense $h$-principle.

nodes.name: Smale-Hirsch immersion theorem
nodes.statement: Using this vocabulary, we can state the Smale-Hirsch immersion theorem as saying that the relation of immersions satisfies all forms of the $h$-principle provided the dimension of the target manifold is larger than the dimension of the source.
assumptions: provided the dimension of the target manifold is larger than the dimension of the source
conclusions: the relation of immersions satisfies all forms of the $h$-principle

nodes.name: the antipodal map turns the sphere inside-out
nodes.statement: The reason why this is turning the sphere inside-out is that $a$ extends as a map from $ℝ^3 ∖ \{0\} → ℝ^3 ∖ \{0\}$ by \[ \hat{a} \co q ↦ -\frac{1}{‖q‖^2}q \] which exchanges the interior and exterior of $𝕊^2$. More abstractly, one can say the normal bundle of $𝕊^2$ is trivial, hence one can extend $a$ to a tubular neighborhood of $𝕊^2$ as an orientation preserving map. Since $a$ is orientation reversing, any such extension will be reversing co-orientation.
nodes.statement_short: The antipodal map extends to $q↦-q/‖q‖^2$, swapping inside and outside of $𝕊^2$, so the eversion turns the sphere inside-out.

nodes.name: Proof of the sphere eversion corollary
nodes.statement: We denote by $ι$ the inclusion of $𝕊^2$ into $ℝ^3$. We set $j_t = (1-t)ι + ta$. This is a homotopy from $ι$ to $a$ (but not an immersion for $t=1/2$). We need to check there is no obstruction to building a homotopy of formal solutions above those maps. One could show that the relevant homotopy group (replacing $π_1(𝕊^1)$ from the Whitney--Graustein example) is $\pi_2(\SO_3(ℝ))$. This group is trivial, hence there is no obstruction. But actually we can write an explicit homotopy here, without computing $\pi_2(\SO_3(ℝ))$. Using the canonical trivialization of the tangent bundle of $ℝ^3$, we can set, for $(q, v) ∈ T𝕊^2$, $G_t(q, v) = \mathrm{Rot}_{Oq}^{πt}(v)$, the rotation around axis $Oq$ with angle $πt$. The family $σ \co t ↦ (j_t, G_t)$ is a homotopy of formal immersions relating $j^1ι$ to $j^1a$. The above theorem ensures this family is homotopic, relative to $t = 0$ and $t = 1$, to a family of holonomic formal immersions, ie a family $t ↦ j^1f_t$ with $f_0 = ι$, $f_1 = a$, and each $f_t$ is an immersion.
nodes.statement_short: Straight-line homotopy $j_t$ from inclusion to antipodal map, lifted to formal immersions by rotations $G_t$; the h-principle then gives a holonomic family.

nodes.name: corrugation achieves the wished derivative (introduction)
nodes.statement: For some large positive $N$, we replace $f$ by the new map \[ x ↦ f(x) + \frac1N ∫_0^{Nx_j} \left[γ_x(s) - ∂_jf(x)\right]ds. \] A wonderfully easy exercise shows that, provided $N$ is large enough, we have achieved $∂_j f(x) ∈ Ω_x$, almost without modifying derivatives $∂_i f(x)$ for $i ≠ j$, and almost without moving $f(x)$.
nodes.statement_short: Corrugating $f$ along $x_j$ with a large frequency $N$ puts $∂_jf$ into $Ω_x$ while barely changing $f$ and the other partials.
assumptions: provided $N$ is large enough
conclusions: we have achieved $∂_j f(x) ∈ Ω_x$, almost without modifying derivatives $∂_i f(x)$ for $i ≠ j$, and almost without moving $f(x)$

nodes.name: ample relation (introduction)
nodes.statement: A relation $\Rel ⊂ J^1(M, N)$ is ample if, for every $(x, y, φ) ∈ \Rel$ and every hyperplane $H ⊂ T_xM$, the convex hull of the connected component of $φ$ in \[ \left\{ψ ∈ \Hom(T_xM, T_yN) \;|\; \rst{ψ}{H} = \rst{φ}{H} \text{ and } (x, y, ψ) ∈ \Rel\right\} \] is the whole set of $ψ$ such that $\rst{ψ}{H} = \rst{φ}{H}$.
nodes.statement_short: A relation is ample if, for each hyperplane, the convex hull of each connected component of the allowed derivatives agreeing on it is everything.

nodes.name: E and F finite-dimensional real vector spaces
nodes.statement: Throughout this document, $E$ and $F$ will denote finite-dimensional real vector spaces.

nodes.name: loop, average of a loop, support of a family of loops
nodes.statement: A loop is a map defined on the circle $𝕊^1 = ℝ/ℤ$ with values in a finite-dimensional vector space. It can also freely be seen as $1$-periodic maps defined on $ℝ$. The average of a loop $γ$ is $\bar γ := \int_{𝕊^1} γ(s)\, ds$. The \emph{support} of a family $γ$ of loops in $F$ parametrized by $E$ is the closure of the set of $x$ in $E$ such that $γ_x$ is not a constant loop.
nodes.label: def:loop

nodes.name: loop construction proposition
nodes.statement: Let $K$ a compact set in $E$. Let $Ω$ be an open set in $E × F$. Let $β$ and $g$ be smooth maps from $E$ to $F$. Write $Ω_x := \{ y ∈ F \mid (x, y) ∈ Ω\}$, assume that $β(x) ∈ Ω_x$ for all $x$, and that $g(x) = β(x)$ near $K$. If, for every $x$, $g(x)$ is in the convex hull of the connected component of $Ω_x$ containing $β(x)$, then there exists a smooth family of loops \[ γ \co E × [0, 1] × 𝕊^1 → F, (x, t, s) ↦ γ^t_x(s) \] such that, for all $x ∈ E$, all $t ∈ ℝ$ and all $s ∈ 𝕊^1$, \begin{itemize} \item $γ^t_x(s) ∈ Ω_x$ \item $γ^0_x(s) = γ^t_x(1) = β(x)$ \item $\bar γ^1_x = g(x)$ \item $γ^t_x(s) = β(x)$ if $x$ is near $K$. \end{itemize}
nodes.statement_short: If $g(x)$ lies in the convex hull of the component of $Ω_x$ containing $β(x)$, there is a smooth family of loops in $Ω_x$ based at $β$ with average $g$, constant near $K$.
assumptions: Let $K$ a compact set in $E$.
Let $Ω$ be an open set in $E × F$.
Let $β$ and $g$ be smooth maps from $E$ to $F$.

and that $g(x) = β(x)$ near $K$.
If, for every $x$, $g(x)$ is in the convex hull of the connected component of $Ω_x$ containing $β(x)$,
conclusions: then there exists a smooth family of loops
nodes.label: prop:∃_loops

nodes.name: Sketch of the loop construction proposition
nodes.statement: Let us briefly sketch the geometric idea behind the above proposition if we pretend there is only one point $x$, and drop it from the notation, and also focus only on $γ^1$. By assumption, there is a finite collection of points $p_i$ in $Ω$ and $λ_i ∈ [0, 1]$ such that $g$ is the barycenter $\sum λ_i p_i$. Since $Ω$ is open and connected, there is a smooth loop $γ_0$ which goes through each $p_i$. The claim is that $g$ is the average value of $γ = γ_0 ∘ h$ for some self-diffeomorphism $h$ of $𝕊^1$. The idea is to choose $h$ such that $γ$ rushes to $p_1$, stays there during a time roughly $λ_1$, rushes to $p_2$, etc. But, in order to achieve average exactly $g$, it seems like $h$ needs to be a discontinuous piecewise constant map. The assumption that $Ω$ is open means that the convex hull is open, which gives enough slack to get away with a smooth $h$.
nodes.statement_short: Proof sketch: pass a loop through barycentric points $p_i$ and reparametrize it to linger near each $p_i$; openness gives slack for a smooth reparametrization.

nodes.name: dimension d of E
nodes.statement: In this section, $E$ is a real vector space with (finite) dimension $d$.

nodes.name: point surrounded by points
nodes.statement: A point $x$ in $E$ is surrounded by points $p_0$, \dots, $p_d$ if those points are affinely independent and there exist weights $w_i ∈ (0, 1)$ with sum $1$ such that $x = \sum_i w_i p_i$.
differentia: there exist weights $w_i ∈ (0, 1)$ with sum $1$ such that $x = \sum_i w_i p_i$
nodes.label: def:surrounds_points

nodes.name: surrounding weights are barycentric coordinates
nodes.statement: Note that, in the above definition, the number of points $p_i$ is fixed by the dimension $d$ of $E$, and that the weights $w_i$ are the barycentric coordinates of $x$ with respect to the affine basis $p_0, \ldots, p_d$.

nodes.name: smooth barycentric coordinates
nodes.statement: For every $x$ in $E$ and every collection of points $p ∈ E^{d+1}$ surrounding $x$, there is a function $w \co E × E^{d+1} → ℝ^{d+1}$ such that, for every $(y, q)$ in a neighborhood of $(x, p)$, \begin{itemize} \item $w$ is smooth at $(y, q)$ \item $w(y, q) > 0$ \item $\sum_{i=0}^d w_i(y, q) = 1$ \item $y = \sum_{i=0}^d w_i(y, q)q_i$. \end{itemize}
nodes.statement_short: Surrounding is locally stable: barycentric weights depend smoothly and stay positive near a surrounding configuration.
assumptions: every collection of points $p ∈ E^{d+1}$ surrounding $x$
conclusions: there is a function $w \co E × E^{d+1} → ℝ^{d+1}$ such that, for every $(y, q)$ in a neighborhood of $(x, p)$,

nodes.name: Proof of smooth barycentric coordinates
nodes.statement: Let: \begin{align*} A = E \times \{ q \in E^{d+1} ~|~ \mbox{$q$ is an affine basis for $E$} \}, \end{align*} and define: \begin{align*} w \co A &\to ℝ^{d+1}\\ (y, q) &\mapsto \mbox{barycentric coordinates of $y$ with respect to $q$}. \end{align*} If we fix an affine basis $b$ of $E$, we may express $w$ as a ratio of determinants in terms of coordinates relative to $b$. More precisely, by Cramer's rule, if $0 \le i \le d$ and $w_i$ is the $i^{\rm th}$ component of $w$, then: \begin{align*} w_i (y, q) = \det M_i (y, q) / \det N (q) \end{align*} where $N(q)$ is the $(d+1)\times (d+1)$ matrix whose columns are the barycentric coordinates of the components of $q$ relative to $b$, and $M_i (y, q)$ is $N(q)$ except with column $i$ replaced by the barycentric coordinates of $y$ relative to $b$. Since determinants are smooth functions and $(y, q) \mapsto \det N(q)$ is non-vanishing on $A$, $w$ is smooth on $A$. Finally define: \begin{align*} U = w^{-1}((0, \infty)^{d+1}), \end{align*} and note that $U$ is open in $A$, since it is the preimage of an open set under the continuous map $w$. In fact since $A$ is open, $U$ is open as a subset of $E \times E^{d+1}$. Note that $(x, p) \in U$ since $p$ surrounds $x$. We may extend $w$ to $E \times E^{d+1}$ by giving it any values at all outside $A$.
nodes.statement_short: Express barycentric coordinates by Cramer's rule as ratios of determinants, hence smooth on the open set of affine bases; positivity is an open condition.

nodes.name: square vertices counterexample
nodes.statement: The first temptation is to hope that $x$ being in the interior of the convex hull of $P$ is enough. But this is not true. For instance the center of a square in a plane is in the interior of the convex hull of the set $P$ of vertices of the square, but it isn't surrounded by any set of vertices.
nodes.statement_short: The center of a square is in the interior of the hull of its vertices but is surrounded by no set of vertices.

nodes.name: Carathéodory's lemma
nodes.statement: If a point $x$ of $E$ lies in the convex hull of a set $P$, then $x$ belongs to the convex hull of a finite set of affinely independent points of $P$.
assumptions: If a point $x$ of $E$ lies in the convex hull of a set $P$,
conclusions: then $x$ belongs to the convex hull of a finite set of affinely independent points of $P$.
nodes.label: lem:caratheodory

nodes.name: Proof of Carathéodory's lemma
nodes.statement: By assumption, there is a finite set of points $t_i$ in $P$ and weights $f_i$ such that $x = \sum f_i t_i$, each $f_i$ is non-negative and $\sum f_i = 1$. Choose such a set of points of minimum cardinality. We argue by contradiction that such a set must be affinely independent. Thus suppose that there is some vanishing combination $\sum g_i t_i$ with $\sum g_i = 0$ and not all $g_i$ vanish. Let $S = \{i | g_i > 0\}$. Let $i_0$ in $S$ be an index minimizing $f_i/g_i$. We shall obtain our contradiction by showing that $x$ belongs to the convex hull of the set $\{t_i| i \ne i_0\}$, which has cardinality strictly smaller than $\{t_i\}$. We thus define new weights $k_i = f_i - g_i f_{i_0}/g_{i_0}$. These weights sum to $\sum f_i - (\sum g_i)f_{i_0}/g_{i_0} = 1$ and $k_{i_0} = 0$. Each $k_i$ is non-negative, thanks to the choice of $i_0$ if $i$ is in $S$ or using that $f_i$, $-g_i$ and $f_{i_0}/g_{i_0}$ are all non-negative when $i$ is not in $S$. It remain to compute \begin{align*} \sum_{i ≠ i_0} k_i t_i &= \sum_i k_i t_i \\ &= \sum_i (f_i - g_i f_{i_0}/g_{i_0}) t_i \\ &= \sum_i f_i t_i - \left(\sum_i g_i t_i\right)f_{i_0}/g_{i_0}) \\ &= x \end{align*} where we use $k_{i_0} = 0$ in the first equality.
nodes.statement_short: Minimal-cardinality convex combination; a nontrivial affine dependence lets one remove a point, contradicting minimality.

nodes.name: Take a minimal convex combination and argue by contradiction
nodes.statement: By assumption, there is a finite set of points $t_i$ in $P$ and weights $f_i$ such that $x = \sum f_i t_i$, each $f_i$ is non-negative and $\sum f_i = 1$. Choose such a set of points of minimum cardinality. We argue by contradiction that such a set must be affinely independent.
nodes.statement_short: Take a minimal convex combination and argue by contradiction

nodes.name: Assume an affine dependence; choose $i_0$ minimizing $f_i/g_i$
nodes.statement: Thus suppose that there is some vanishing combination $\sum g_i t_i$ with $\sum g_i = 0$ and not all $g_i$ vanish. Let $S = \{i | g_i > 0\}$. Let $i_0$ in $S$ be an index minimizing $f_i/g_i$. We shall obtain our contradiction by showing that $x$ belongs to the convex hull of the set $\{t_i| i \ne i_0\}$, which has cardinality strictly smaller than $\{t_i\}$.
nodes.statement_short: Assume an affine dependence; choose $i_0$ minimizing $f_i/g_i$

nodes.name: New weights $k_i$ summing to 1 with $k_{i_0}=0$
nodes.statement: We thus define new weights $k_i = f_i - g_i f_{i_0}/g_{i_0}$. These weights sum to $\sum f_i - (\sum g_i)f_{i_0}/g_{i_0} = 1$ and $k_{i_0} = 0$.

nodes.name: The new weights are non-negative
nodes.statement: Each $k_i$ is non-negative, thanks to the choice of $i_0$ if $i$ is in $S$ or using that $f_i$, $-g_i$ and $f_{i_0}/g_{i_0}$ are all non-negative when $i$ is not in $S$.
nodes.statement_short: The new weights are non-negative

nodes.name: They still represent $x$, contradicting minimality

nodes.name: interior of convex hull of an affine basis
nodes.statement: Given an affine basis $b$ of $E$, the interior of the convex hull of $b$ is the set of points with strictly positive barycentric coordinates.
assumptions: Given an affine basis $b$ of $E$,
conclusions: the interior of the convex hull of $b$ is the set of points with strictly positive barycentric coordinates.
nodes.label: lem:interior_chab

nodes.name: Proof of interior of convex hull of an affine basis
nodes.statement: For each $i$, let: \[ w_i \co E \to ℝ \] be the $i^{\rm th}$ barycentric coordinate with respect to the basis $b$. Since $E$ is finite-dimensional, each $w_i$ is a continuous open map. For such a map, the operation of taking interior commutes with preimage, and so we have: \begin{align*} \IntConv(b) &= \Int\left(\bigcap_i w_i^{-1}([0, \infty))\right)\\ &= \bigcap_i \Int(w_i^{-1}([0, \infty))\\ &= \bigcap_i w_i^{-1}(\Int([0, \infty))\\ &= \bigcap_i w_i^{-1}((0, \infty)) \end{align*} as required.
nodes.statement_short: Barycentric coordinates are continuous open maps, so interior commutes with preimage.

nodes.name: dilation of a convex set about an interior point
nodes.statement: Given a point $c$ of $E$ and a real number $t$, let: \[ h^c_t \co E \to E \] be the homothety which dilates about $c$ by a scale of $t$. Suppose $c$ belongs to the interior of a convex subset $C$ of $E$ and $t > 1$, then \[ C \subseteq \Int(h^c_t(C)) \]
assumptions: Suppose $c$ belongs to the interior of a convex subset $C$ of $E$
conclusions: \[ C \subseteq \Int(h^c_t(C)) \]

nodes.name: Proof of dilation lemma
nodes.statement: Since $h^c_t$ is a homeomorphism with inverse $h^c_{t^{-1}}$, taking $s = t^{-1}$, the required result is equivalent to showing: \[ h^c_s(C) \subseteq \Int(C) \] where $s \in (0, 1)$. Indeed $U$ is open since $h^x_{1-s}$ is a homeomorphism and $U$ contains $h^c_s(x)$ since: \[ h^c_s(x) = h^x_{1-s}(c) \in h^x_{1-s}(\Int(C)) \] since $c$ belongs to $\Int(C)$. Finally: \[ h^x_{1-s}(\Int(C)) \subseteq h^x_{1-s}(C) \subseteq C \] where the second inclusion follows since $C$ is convex and contains $x$.

nodes.name: Proof of points in the convex hull of an open set are surrounded
nodes.statement: It follows from \Cref{lem:interior_chab} that we need only show that $E$ has an affine basis $b$ of points belonging to $P$ such that $x$ lies in the interior of the convex hull of $b$. Carathéodory's lemma~\ref{lem:caratheodory} provides affinely independent points $p_0, \dots, p_k$ in $P$ such that $x$ belongs to their convex hull. Since $P$ is open, we may extend $p_i$ to an affine basis \[ \hat b = \{p_0, \ldots, p_d\}, \] where all points still belong to $P$. Note that $x$ belongs to the convex hull of $\hat b$. Now let $c$ be a point in the interior of the convex hull of $\hat b$ (e.g., the centroid) and for each $\epsilon > 0$, consider the homothety \[ h_{1+\epsilon} \co E \to E, \] which dilates about $c$ by a scale of $1 + \epsilon$. Since $\hat b$ is finite and contained in $P$, and $P$ is open, there exists $\epsilon > 0$ such that \[ h_{1+\epsilon} (\hat b) \subseteq P. \] We claim the required basis is: \[ b = h_{1+\epsilon} (\hat b) \] for any such $\epsilon$. Indeed, applying \Cref{lem:int_homothety_cvx} to $\Conv(\hat b)$ we see: \begin{align*} x \in \Conv(\hat b) &\subseteq \Int (h_{1+\epsilon} (\Conv(\hat b)))\\ &= \Int (\Conv(h_{1+\epsilon} (\hat b))) \end{align*} as required.
nodes.statement_short: Use Carathéodory to get affinely independent points, extend to an affine basis in $P$, and dilate slightly so $x$ lies in the interior of the hull.

nodes.name: loop surrounding a vector; based loop
nodes.statement: We say a loop $γ$ surrounds a vector $v$ if $v$ is surrounded by a collection of points belonging to the image of $γ$. Also, we fix a base point $0$ in $𝕊^1$ and say a loop is based at some point $b$ if $0$ is sent to $b$.
nodes.label: def:surrounds

nodes.name: loop of hull
nodes.statement: If a vector $v$ is in the convex hull of a connected open subset $O$ then, for every base point $b ∈ O$, there is a continuous family of loops $γ \co [0, 1] × 𝕊^1 → E, (t, s) ↦ γ^t(s)$ such that, for all $t$ and $s$: \begin{itemize} \item $γ^t$ is based at $b$ \item $γ^0(s) = b$ \item $γ^t(s) ∈ O$ \item $γ^1$ surrounds $v$ \end{itemize}
assumptions: If a vector $v$ is in the convex hull of a connected open subset $O$
for every base point $b ∈ O$,
conclusions: there is a continuous family of loops $γ \co [0, 1] × 𝕊^1 → E, (t, s) ↦ γ^t(s)$ such that, for all $t$ and $s$:
nodes.label: lem:loop_of_hull

nodes.name: Proof of loop of hull
nodes.statement: Since $O$ is open, \Cref{prop:surrounded_by_open} gives points $p_i$ in $O$ surrounding $x$. Since $O$ is open and connected, it is path connected. Let $λ \co [0, 1] → Ω_x$ be a continuous path starting at $b$ and going through the points $p_i$. We can concatenate $λ$ and its opposite to get $γ^1$. This is a round-trip loop: it back-tracks when it reaches $λ(1)$ at $s = 1/2$. We then define $γ^t$ as the round-trip that stops at $s = t/2$, stays still until $s = 1-t/2$ and then backtracks.
nodes.statement_short: Get surrounding points, join them by a path from $b$, take the round-trip loop and truncate it for $t<1$.

nodes.name: Get points $p_i$ in $O$ surrounding $v$
nodes.statement: Since $O$ is open, \Cref{prop:surrounded_by_open} gives points $p_i$ in $O$ surrounding $x$.

nodes.name: local surrounding loops

If $g(x_0)$ is in the convex hull of the connected component of $Ω_{x_0}$ containing $β(x_0)$,
conclusions: then there is a continuous family of loops defined near $x_0$, based at $β$, taking value in $Ω$ and surrounding $g$.

nodes.name: Proof of local surrounding loops
nodes.statement: In this proof we don't mention the $t$ parameter since it plays no role, but it is still there. \Cref{lem:loop_of_hull} gives a loop $γ$ based at $β(x_0)$, taking values in $Ω_{x_0}$ and surrounding $g(x_0)$. We set $γ_x(s) = β(x) + (γ(s) - β(x_0))$. Each $γ_x$ takes values in $Ω_x$ because $Ω$ is open over some neighborhood of $x_0$. \Cref{lem:smooth_barycentric_coord} guarantees that this loop surrounds $g(x)$ for $x$ close enough to $x_0$.

nodes.name: satisfied or refund
nodes.statement: For every set $U ⊂ E$, $\Loop(g, β, U, Ω)$ is ``path connected'': for every $γ_0$ and $γ_1$ in $\Loop(g, β, U, Ω)$, there is a continuous map $δ \co [0, 1] × E × [0, 1] × 𝕊^1 → F, (τ, x, t, s) ↦ δ^t_{τ, x}(s)$ which interpolates between $γ_0$ and $γ_1$ in $\Loop(g, β, U, Ω)$.
nodes.statement_short: Any two surrounding loop families can be joined by a continuous path of surrounding loop families.
assumptions: For every set $U ⊂ E$,
for every $γ_0$ and $γ_1$ in $\Loop(g, β, U, Ω)$,
conclusions: $\Loop(g, β, U, Ω)$ is ``path connected''
there is a continuous map $δ \co [0, 1] × E × [0, 1] × 𝕊^1 → F, (τ, x, t, s) ↦ δ^t_{τ, x}(s)$ which interpolates between $γ_0$ and $γ_1$ in $\Loop(g, β, U, Ω)$.
nodes.label: lem:satisfied_or_refund

nodes.name: Proof of satisfied or refund
nodes.statement: Let $ρ$ be the piecewise affine map from $ℝ$ to $ℝ$ such that $ρ(τ) = 1$ if $τ ≤ 1/2$, $ρ$ is affine on $[1/2, 1]$, $ρ(τ) = 0$ if $τ ≥ 1$. We set \[ δ_{τ, x}^t(s) = \begin{cases} γ_{0,x}^{ρ(τ)t}\left(\frac1{1 - τ} s\right) & \text{if $s ≤ 1 - τ$ and $τ < 1$}\\ γ_{1,x}^{ρ(1-τ)t}\left(\frac1τ \big(s - (1- τ)\big)\right) & \text{if $s ≥ 1 - τ$ and $τ > 0$}\\ \end{cases} \] It is clear that if $s = 1 - τ$ then both branches agree and are equal to $β(x)$. Therefore it is easy to see that $δ$ is continuous at $(τ, x, t, s)$ except when $(τ,s)=(1,0)$ or $(τ,s)=(0,1)$. To show the continuity for $(τ,s)=(1,0)$, let $K$ be a compact neighborhood of $x$ in $E$. Then $γ_0$ is uniformly continuous on the compact set $K × [0, 1] × 𝕊^1$, which means that $γ_{0,x'}^t$ tends uniformly to the constant function $s ↦ β(x)$ as $(x', t)$ tends to $(x, 0)$. This means that $γ_{0,x'}^{ρ(τ)t'}$ tends uniformly to the constant function $s ↦ β(x)$ as $(τ, x', t')$ tends to $(1, x, t)$. This means that $δ$ is continuous at $(τ,s)=(1,0)$ (it is clear that the other branch also tends to $β(x)$). The continuity at $(τ,s)=(0,1)$ is entirely analogous. The beautiful observation motivating the above formula is why each $δ_{τ, x}^1$ surrounds $g(x)$. The key is that the image of $δ_{τ, x}^1$ contains the image of $γ_{0,x}^1$ when $τ ≤ 1/2$, and contains the image of $γ_{1,x}^1$ when $τ ≥ 1/2$. Hence $δ_{τ, x}^1$ always surrounds $g(x)$.
nodes.statement_short: Explicit interpolation concatenating shrunken pieces of the two loops; continuity at corner parameters by uniform continuity, and the image always contains one full $γ^1$.

nodes.statement: Let $U_0$ and $U_1$ be open sets in $E$. Let $K_0 ⊂ U_0$ and $K_1 ⊂ U_1$ be compact subsets. For any $γ_0 ∈ \Loop(U_0, g, β, Ω)$ and $γ_1 ∈ \Loop(U_1, g, β, Ω)$, there exists a neighborhood $U$ of $K_0 ∪ K_1$ and there exists $γ ∈ \Loop(U, g, β, Ω)$ which coincides with $γ_0$ near $K_0\cup U_1^c$.

For any $γ_0 ∈ \Loop(U_0, g, β, Ω)$ and $γ_1 ∈ \Loop(U_1, g, β, Ω)$,

nodes.name: Proof of extending surrounding loops
nodes.statement: Let $C_0 = K_0\cup U_1^c$ and $C_1 := K_1 ∖ U_0$. Since $C_0$ and $C_1$ are disjoint closed sets, there is some continuous cut-off $ρ \co E → [0, 1]$ which vanishes on a neighborhood of $C_0$ and equals one on a neighborhood of $C_1$. \Cref{lem:satisfied_or_refund} gives a homotopy of loops $γ_τ$ from $γ_0$ to $γ_1$ on $U_0 ∩ U_1$. Moreover, note that $γ_τ$ is defined on all of $E$. On $U_0' ∪ (U_0 ∩ U_1) ∪ U_1'$, which is a neighborhood of $K_0 ∪ K_1$, we set \[ γ_x = γ_{ρ(x), x} \] which has the required properties.
nodes.statement_short: Glue the two families with a cut-off along the satisfied-or-refund homotopy.

nodes.statement: Let $C_0 = K_0\cup U_1^c$ and $C_1 := K_1 ∖ U_0$. Since $C_0$ and $C_1$ are disjoint closed sets, there is some continuous cut-off $ρ \co E → [0, 1]$ which vanishes on a neighborhood of $C_0$ and equals one on a neighborhood of $C_1$.

nodes.name: global smooth function from local ones for convex constraints
nodes.statement: Let $E$ and $F$ be real normed vector spaces. Assume that $E$ is finite dimensional. Let $P$ be a predicate on $E \times F$ such that for all $x$ in $E$, $\{y ~|~ P (x, y) \}$ is convex. Let $n$ be a natural number or $+\infty$. Assume that every $x$ has a neighbourhood $U$ on which there exists a $\C^n$ function $f$ such that $\forall x ∈ U, P(x, f(x))$. Then there is a global $\C^n$ function $f$ such that $\forall x, P(x, f(x))$.
nodes.statement_short: Convex pointwise constraints with local $C^n$ solutions admit a global $C^n$ solution.

nodes.name: Proof of global smooth function from local ones

Let $ρ$ be a smooth partition of unity associated to this cover. The function $f = ∑ ρ_i f_i$ is smooth on $E$ and the convexity assumption on $P$ ensures it satisfies $\forall x, P(x, f(x))$. nodes.name: reparametrization lemma
nodes.statement: Let $γ \co E × 𝕊^1 → F$ be a smooth family of loops surrounding a map $g$. There is a smooth family $φ \co E × 𝕊^1 → 𝕊^1$ such that each $γ_x ∘ φ_x$ has average $g(x)$ and $φ_x(0) = 0$.

conclusions: There is a smooth family $φ \co E × 𝕊^1 → 𝕊^1$ such that each $γ_x ∘ φ_x$ has average $g(x)$ and $φ_x(0) = 0$.

nodes.name: Proof of the reparametrization lemma
nodes.statement: Gromov's main idea in order to prove this result is to translate the problem of constructing a family of circle maps $φ$ into the problem of constructing a family of smooth density functions $f$ on the circle. We introduce some vocabulary in order to describe this reduction. Let $f \co E × ℝ → ℝ$ be a smooth positive function that is $1$-periodic in its second argument. We say that $f$ is a centering density for $(γ, g)$ at $x$ if $f_x \co ℝ → ℝ$ has average value one when seen as a function on $𝕊¹$ and the average value of $f_x γ_x$ is $g(x)$. We claim that, in order to prove the lemma, it is sufficient to build such an $f$ which is centering at every $x$. Indeed, assume we have such an $f$. We then get a smooth family of $ℤ$-equivariant functions $ψ \co E × ℝ → ℝ$ defined by $ψ_x(t) = \int_0^tf_x(s)ds$. Because $ψ$ is smooth and each $ψ_x$ is strictly monotone and $ℤ$-equivariant, one can check there is a smooth map $φ : E × ℝ → ℝ$ which is $ℤ$-equivariant and such that $φ_x ∘ ψ_x = \Id$ for each $x$. Seen as a family of functions from $𝕊¹$ to $𝕊¹$, those functions are suitable since, for every $x$, the change of variable formula gives: \[ \int_{𝕊¹} γ_x ∘ φ_x(s)ds = \int_{𝕊¹} ψ_x'(s) γ_x ∘ φ_x(ψ_x(s))ds = \int_{𝕊¹} f_x(s) γ_x(s)ds = g(x). \] We now prove the existence of a function which is a centering density at every point of $x$. For any given $x$, this constraint is clearly convex. Hence \Cref{lem:exists_cont_diff_of_convex₂} ensures it is enough to prove existence of functions that are centering densities in a neighborhood of any given point $x$. So we fix some $x$ in $E$. Since $γ_x$ strictly surrounds $g(x)$, there are points $s_1, …, s_{n+1}$ in $𝕊^1$ such that $g(x)$ is surrounded by the corresponding points $γ_x(s_j)$. Let $f_1, …, f_{n+1}$ be smooth positive periodic maps from $ℝ$ to $ℝ$ which average value $1$ on a period and such that the corresponding measures on $𝕊¹$ are very close to the Dirac measures on $s_j$, ie. for any function $h$, the average value of $f_jh$ is almost $h(s_j)$. We set $p_j = \int f_jγ_x\, ds$, which is almost $γ_x(s_j)$ so that $g(x) = \sum w_j p_j$ for some weights $w_j$ in the open interval $(0, 1)$ according to \Cref{lem:smooth_barycentric_coord}. If $x'$ is in a sufficiently small neighborhood of $x$, \Cref{lem:smooth_barycentric_coord} gives smooth weight functions $w_j$ such that $g(x') = \sum w_j(x')p_j(x')$. Hence we can set $f_{x'}(s) = \sum w_j(x')f_j(s)$.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to building centering densities, a convex condition, and build them locally from approximate Dirac densities with smooth barycentric weights. The reduction inverts the primitive of the density to get the circle maps.

nodes.name: Proof of the loop construction proposition
nodes.statement: Let $γ^*$ be a family of loops surrounding the origin in $B_F(0,1)$ the open unit ball in $F$, constructed using \Cref{lem:local_loops}. For $x$ in some neighborhood $U^*$ of $K$ where $g = β$, we set $γ_x = g(x) + εγ^*$ where $ε > 0$ is sufficiently small to ensure that $B_{E\times F}((x,β(x)),2ε)\subseteq \Omega$ (recall $Ω$ is open and $K$ is compact). \Cref{lem:∃_surrounding_loops} extends this family to a continuous family of surrounding loops $γ_x$ for all $x$ (this is not yet our final $γ$). We then need to approximate this continuous family by a smooth one. Some care is needed to ensure that it stays based at $β$. We can first reparametrize $γ$ on $[0,1] \times 𝕊^1$ to ensure that $γ$ is constant in a neighborhood of $C = \{(t, s) \in [0,1] \times 𝕊^1 \mid t = 0 \text{ or } s = 0\}$. Using \Cref{lem:exists_cont_diff_of_convex}, we can find a smooth function that has distance at most $ε$ from $γ$ and coincides with $γ$ on $C$ (using the fact that $γ$ is already smooth near $C$). Since all loops that are sufficiently close to $γ$ still surround $g$, we can also ensure that the new smoothened $γ$ is still surrounding. Then \Cref{lem:reparametrization} gives a family of circle diffeomorphisms $h_x$ such that $γ^1_x ∘ h_x$ has average $g(x)$. Finally we choose a cut-off function function $χ$ which vanishes near $E ∖ U^*$ and equals one near $K$. As our final family of loops, we choose $χ(x)g(x) + (1-χ(x))(γ_x ∘ h_x)$. This operation does not change the average values of these loops, because it rescales them around their average value, but makes them constant near $K$. Also, those loops stay in $Ω$, thanks to our choice of $ε$.

nodes.name: dual pair
nodes.statement: A dual pair on a vector space $E$ is a pair $(π, v)$ where $π$ is a linear form on $E$ and $v$ a vector in $E$ such that $π(v) = 1$.
nodes.label: def:dual_pair

nodes.name: E and F finite dimensional normed spaces (local theory)
nodes.statement: Let $E$ and $F$ be finite dimensional real normed vector spaces.

nodes.name: map f and dual pair (π, v) to corrugate
nodes.statement: Let $f \co E → F$ be a smooth map, and let $(π, v)$ be a dual pair on $E$.

nodes.name: target open sets Ω_x
nodes.statement: Say we wish $Df(x)v$ could live in some open subset $Ω_x ⊂ F$.

nodes.name: family of loops with average Df(x)v
nodes.statement: Assume there is a smooth family of loops $γ \co E × 𝕊^1 → F$ such that each $γ_x$ takes values in $Ω_x$, and its average value $\overline{γ}_x = \int_{𝕊^1} γ_x$ is $Df(x)v$ for all $x$.

nodes.name: corrugation
nodes.statement: The map obtained by corrugation of $f$ in direction $(π, v)$ using $γ$ with oscillation number $N$ is \[ x ↦ f(x) + \frac1N ∫_0^{Nπ(x)} \left[γ_x(s) - \overline{γ}_x\right]ds. \]
nodes.statement_short: Corrugation adds $\frac1N∫_0^{Nπ(x)}(γ_x(s)-\bar γ_x)ds$ to $f(x)$.
nodes.label: def:corrugation

nodes.name: Theillière's corrugation estimates
nodes.statement: Let $f$ be a $\mathcal{C}^1$ function from $E$ to $F$. Let $(π, v)$ be a dual pair on $E$. Let $γ \co E × 𝕊^1 → F$ be a $\mathcal{C}^1$ family of loops such that $\overline{γ_x} = Df(x)v$ for all $x$. For any compact set $K ⊂ E$ and any positive $ε$, the function $f'$ obtained by corrugation of $f$ in direction $(π, v)$ using $γ$ with large enough oscillation number $N$ satisfies: \begin{enumerate} \item $∀ x ∈ K, ‖f'(x) - f(x)‖ ≤ ε$ \item $∀ x ∈ K, ‖(Df'(x) - Df(x))_{|\ker π}‖ ≤ ε$. \item $∀ x ∈ K, ‖Df'(x)v - γ(x, Nπ(x))‖ ≤ ε$ \end{enumerate} In addition, all the differences estimated above vanish if $x$ is outside the support of $γ$.
nodes.statement_short: Corrugation with large $N$ is $C^0$-close to $f$, nearly preserves $Df$ on $\ker π$, and makes $Df'v$ close to $γ(x,Nπ(x))$.

Let $(π, v)$ be a dual pair on $E$.
Let $γ \co E × 𝕊^1 → F$ be a $\mathcal{C}^1$ family of loops such that $\overline{γ_x} = Df(x)v$ for all $x$.
For any compact set $K ⊂ E$ and any positive $ε$,
with large enough oscillation number $N$
conclusions: $∀ x ∈ K, ‖Df'(x)v - γ(x, Nπ(x))‖ ≤ ε$
In addition, all the differences estimated above vanish if $x$ is outside the support of $γ$.

nodes.name: Proof of Theillière's corrugation estimates
nodes.statement: We set $Γ_x(t) = ∫_0^t \left(γ_x(s) - \overline{γ}_x\right)ds$, so that $f'(x) = f(x) + Γ_x(Nπ(x))/N$. Because each $Γ_x$ is $1$-periodic, and everything has compact support in $E$, all derivatives of $Γ$ are uniformly bounded. Item~\ref{CP:C0} in the statement is then obvious. Item~\ref{CP:kerpi} also follows since $∂_if'(x) = ∂_if(x) + ∂_iΓ(x, Nπ(x))/N$. In order to prove Item~\ref{CP:v}, we compute: \begin{align*} Df'(x)v &= Df(x)v + \frac1N ∂_jΓ(x, Nπ(x)) + \frac NN ∂_tΓ(x, Nπ(x))\\ &= Df(x)v + \bigO{\frac1N} + γ(x, Nπ(x)) - Df(x)v\\ &= γ(x, Nπ(x)) + \bigO{\frac1N}. \end{align*} Outside the support of $γ$, $Γ_x$ and its derivative with respect to $x$ vanish identically (for the derivative computation, it is important that the support of $γ$ is the \emph{closure} of the set of $x$ where $γ_x$ is not constant).
nodes.statement_short: Periodicity and compact support bound all derivatives of the primitive $Γ$, giving $O(1/N)$ errors; differentiate along $v$ to recover $γ$.

nodes.name: Primitive $Γ$ is periodic with bounded derivatives
nodes.statement: We set $Γ_x(t) = ∫_0^t \left(γ_x(s) - \overline{γ}_x\right)ds$, so that $f'(x) = f(x) + Γ_x(Nπ(x))/N$. Because each $Γ_x$ is $1$-periodic, and everything has compact support in $E$, all derivatives of $Γ$ are uniformly bounded.
nodes.statement_short: Primitive $Γ$ is periodic with bounded derivatives

nodes.name: Estimate on $\ker π$

nodes.name: Compute $Df'(x)v$
nodes.statement: In order to prove Item~\ref{CP:v}, we compute: \begin{align*} Df'(x)v &= Df(x)v + \frac1N ∂_jΓ(x, Nπ(x)) + \frac NN ∂_tΓ(x, Nπ(x))\\ &= Df(x)v + \bigO{\frac1N} + γ(x, Nπ(x)) - Df(x)v\\ &= γ(x, Nπ(x)) + \bigO{\frac1N}. \end{align*}

nodes.name: Vanishing outside the support
nodes.statement: Outside the support of $γ$, $Γ_x$ and its derivative with respect to $x$ vanish identically (for the derivative computation, it is important that the support of $γ$ is the \emph{closure} of the set of $x$ where $γ_x$ is not constant).

nodes.name: E'-holonomic map
nodes.statement: Let $E'$ be a linear subspace of $E$. A map $\F = (f, φ) : E → F × \Hom(E, F)$ is $E'$--holonomic if, for every $v$ in $E'$ and every $x$, $Df(x)v = φ(x)v$.

nodes.name: first order differential relation (local)
nodes.statement: A first order differential relation for maps from $E$ to $F$ is a subset $\Rel$ of $E × F × \Hom(E, F)$.

nodes.name: convention: R a relation for maps from E to F
nodes.statement: Until the end of this section, $\Rel$ will always denote a first order differential relation for maps from $E$ to $F$.

nodes.name: formal solution (local)
nodes.statement: A formal solution of a differential relation $\Rel$ is a map $\F = (f, φ) \co E → F × \Hom(E, F)$ such that, for every $x$, $(x, f(x), φ(x))$ is in $\Rel$.

nodes.name: base map (local)
nodes.statement: The first component of a map $\F \co E → F × \Hom(E, F)$ will sometimes be denoted by $\bs \F \co E → F$ and called the base map of $\F$.

nodes.name: 1-jet section and homotopy of 1-jet sections

nodes.name: slice of a relation

nodes.name: Proof of the main inductive step
nodes.statement: We denote the components of $\F$ by $f$ and $φ$. Since $\F$ is short, \cref{prop:∃_loops} applied to $g \co x ↦ Df(x)v$, $β \co x ↦ φ(x)v$, $Ω_x = \Rel(\F(x), π, v)$, and $K = C ∩ K_1$ gives us a smooth family of loops $γ \co E × [0, 1] × 𝕊^1 → F$ such that, for all $x$: \begin{itemize} \item $∀ t\, s,\; γ^t_x(s) ∈ \Rel(\F(x), π, v)$ \item $∀ s,\; γ^0_x(s) = φ(x)v$ \item $\bar γ^1_x = Df(x)v$ \item if $x$ is near $C$, $∀t\, s,\; γ^t_x(s) = φ(x)v$ \end{itemize} Let $ρ: E → ℝ$ be a smooth cut-off function which equals one on a neighborhood of $K_0$ and whose support is contained in $K_1$. Let $N$ be a positive real number. Let $\bar f$ be the corrugated map constructed from $f$, $γ^1$ and $N$. \Cref{prop:theilliere} ensures that, for all $x$, \[ D\bar f(x) = Df(x) + \left[γ^1_x(Nπ(x)) - Df(x)v\right] ⊗ π + R_x \] for some remainder term $R$ which is $ε$-small and vanishes whenever $γ_x$ is constant, hence vanishes near $C$. We set $\F_t(x) = \big(f_t(x), φ_t(x)\big)$ where: \[ f_t(x) = f(x) + \frac{tρ(x)}N \int_0^{Nπ(x)} \left[γ^t_x(s) - Df(x)v\right]\, ds \] and \[ φ_t(x) = φ(x) + \left[γ^{tρ(x)}_x(Nπ(x)) - φ(x)v\right] ⊗ π + \frac{tρ(x)}N B_x. \] We now prove that $\F_t$ has the announced properties, starting with he obvious ones. The fact that $\F_0 = \F$ is obvious since $γ^0_x(s) = φ(x)v$ for all $s$. When $x$ is near $C$, $Df(x) = φ(x)$ since $\F$ is holonomic near $C$. In addition, $γ^t_x(s) = φ(x)v$ for all $s$ and $t$, hence $B_x$ vanishes. Hence $\F_t(x) = \F(x)$ for all $t$ when $x$ is near $C$. Outside of $K_1$, $ρ$ vanishes. Hence $f_t(x) = f(x)$ for all $t$, and $γ^{tρ(x)}_x(s) = φ(x)v$ for all $s$ and $t$, and $φ_t(x) = φ(x)$. The distance between $f(x)$ and $f_t(x)$ is zero outside of $K_1$ and $ε$-small everywhere. We now turn to the interesting parts. The first one is that each $\F_t$ is a formal solution of $\Rel$. We already now that $\F_t$ coincides with $\F$, which is a formal solution, outside of the compact set $K_1$. We set \[ \F'_t(x) = \left(f(x), φ(x) + \left[γ^{tρ(x)}_x(Nπ(x)) - φ(x)v\right] ⊗ π\right). \] Since $\Rel$ is open, and $K_1 × [0, 1]$ is compact and $\F_t$ is within $\bigO{1/N}$ of $\F'_t$, it suffices to prove that $\F'_t$ is a formal solution for all $t$. This is guaranteed by the definition of the slice $\Rel(\F(x), π, v)$ to which $γ^{tρ(x)}_x(Nπ(x))$ belongs. Finally, let's prove that $\F_1$ is $E' ⊕ ℝv$--holonomic near $K_0$. Since $ρ = 1$ near $K_0$, we have, for $x$ near $K_0$, \[ Df_1(x) = Df(x) + \left[γ^1_x(Nπ(x)) - Df(x)v\right] ⊗ π + \frac1N B_x, \] and \[ φ_1(x) = φ(x) + \left[γ^1_x(Nπ(x)) - φ(x)v\right] ⊗ π + \frac{1}N B_x. \] Let $p$ be the projection of $E$ onto $\ker π$ along $v$, so that $\Id_E = p + v ⊗ π$. We can rewrite the above formulas as \[ Df_1(x) = Df(x) ∘ p + γ^1_x(Nπ(x)) ⊗ π + \frac1N B_x, \] and \[ φ_1(x) = φ(x) ∘ p + γ^1_x(Nπ(x)) ⊗ π + \frac{1}N B_x. \] So we see the difference is $Df(x) ∘ p - φ(x) ∘ p$ which vanishes on $E'$ since $\F$ is $E'$--holonomic near $K_0$, and vanishes on $v$ since $p(v) = 0$.
nodes.statement_short: Apply the loop construction to the slices, corrugate $f$ with the loops and cut off; openness and the corrugation estimates give formal solutions, and a projection computation gives the new holonomy.

Since $ρ = 1$ near $K_0$, we have, for $x$ near $K_0$, \[ Df_1(x) = Df(x) + \left[γ^1_x(Nπ(x)) - Df(x)v\right] ⊗ π + \frac1N B_x, \] and \[ φ_1(x) = φ(x) + \left[γ^1_x(Nπ(x)) - φ(x)v\right] ⊗ π + \frac{1}N B_x. \] Let $p$ be the projection of $E$ onto $\ker π$ along $v$, so that $\Id_E = p + v ⊗ π$. We can rewrite the above formulas as \[ Df_1(x) = Df(x) ∘ p + γ^1_x(Nπ(x)) ⊗ π + \frac1N B_x, \] and \[ φ_1(x) = φ(x) ∘ p + γ^1_x(Nπ(x)) ⊗ π + \frac{1}N B_x. \] So we see the difference is $Df(x) ∘ p - φ(x) ∘ p$ which vanishes on $E'$ since $\F$ is $E'$--holonomic near $K_0$, and vanishes on $v$ since $p(v) = 0$.

nodes.name: Proof that complements of codimension-two subspaces are ample
nodes.statement: Let $F$ be subspace of $E$ with codimension at least $2$. Let $F'$ be a complement subspace. Its dimension is at least $2$ since it is isomorphic to $E/F$ and $\dim(E/F) = \codim(F) ≥ 2$. First note the complement of $F$ is path-connected. Indeed let $x$ and $y$ be points outside $F$. Decomposing on $F ⊕ F'$, we get $x = u + u'$ and $y = v + v'$ with $u' ≠ 0$ and $v' ≠ 0$. The segments from $x$ to $u'$ and $y$ to $v'$ stay outside $F$, so it suffices to connect $u'$ and $v'$ in $F' ∖ \{0\}$. If the segment from $u'$ to $v'$ doesn't contains the origin then we are done. Otherwise $v' = μu'$ for some (negative) $u'$. Since $\dim(F') ≥ 2$ and $u' ≠ 0$, there exists $f ∈ F'$ which is linearly independent from $u'$, hence from $v'$. We can then connect both $u'$ and $v'$ to $f$ by a segment away from zero. We now turn to ampleness. The connectedness result reduces to prove that every $e$ in $E$ is in the convex hull of $E ∖ F$. If $e$ is not in $F$ then it is the convex combination of itself with coefficient $1$ and we are done. Now assume $e$ is in $F$. The codimension assumption guarantees the existence of a subspace $G$ such that $\dim(G) = 2$ and $G ∩ F = \{0\}$. Let $(g_1, g_2)$ be a basis of $G$. We set $p_1 = e + g_1$, $p_2 = e + g_2$, $p_3 = e - g_1 - g_2$. All these points are in $E ∖ F$ and $e = p_1/3 + p_2/3 + p_3/3$.
nodes.statement_short: Show the complement is path-connected by going around the origin in a complement plane, then write each point as a barycenter of three points off the subspace.

nodes.name: Proof of local h-principle
nodes.statement: This is a straightforward induction using \cref{lem:integration_step}. Let $(e_1, \dots, e_n)$ be a basis of $E$, and let $(π_1, \dots, π_n)$ be the dual basis. Let $E'_i$ be the linear subspace of $E$ spanned by $(e_1, \dots, e_i)$, for $1 ≤ i ≤ n$, and let $E'_0$ be the zero subspace of $E$. Each $(π_i, e_i)$ is a dual pair and the kernel of $π_i$ contains $E'_{i - 1}$. \Cref{lem:integration_step} allows to build a sequence of homotopies of formal solutions, each homotopy relating a formal solution which is $E'_i$--holonomic to one which is $E'_{i+1}$--holonomic (always near $K_0$). The shortness condition is always satisfies because $\Rel$ is ample. Each homotopy starts where the previous one stopped, stay at $C^0$ distance at most $ε/n$, and is relative to $C$ and the complement of $K_1$. It then suffices to do a smooth concatenation of theses homotopies. We first pre-compose with a smooth map from $[0, 1]$ to itself that fixes $0$ and $1$ and has vanishing derivative to all orders at $0$ and $1$. Then we precompose by affine isomorphisms from $[0, 1]$ to $[i/n, (i + 1)/n]$ before joining them.
nodes.statement_short: Induction over a basis applying the integration step once per coordinate direction, then smoothly concatenate the homotopies.

nodes.statement: Here a smooth open embedding from a manifold $X$ to a manifold $Y$ is a smooth map $φ : X → Y$ which is open and for which there is some smooth $ψ : φ(X) → X$ such that $ψ ∘ φ = \Id_X$ (hence also and $φ ∘ ψ = \Id_{φ(X)}$).

nodes.name: locally finite family of sets
nodes.statement: Remember that a family of sets $V_i$ in a topological space $X$ is locally finite if every point of $X$ has a neighborhood that intersects only finitely many $V_i$.

nodes.name: Proof of nice atlas
nodes.statement: The proof is a standard compact-exhaustion argument. Let $K_0, K_1, K_2, \ldots $ be a compact exhaustion of $M$ and define: \begin{align*} C_n &= K_{n+2} \smallsetminus K_{n+1}^o,\\ U_n &= K_{n+3}^o \smallsetminus K_n. \end{align*} Thus: \begin{itemize} \item $C_n$ is compact, \item $U_n$ is open, \item $C_n \subseteq U_n$, \item $\bigcup_n C_n = M$, \item $U_n \cap U_m = \emptyset$ if $|n - m| > 2$. \end{itemize} For any $y \in E$ and $r > 0$, fix a smooth diffeomorphism $f_{y,r} : E \simeq B_E(y, r)$ such that $f_{y,r}(0) = y$. For each $n$ and $x \in C_n$, let $\psi_x$ be a smooth chart mapping an open neighbourhood of $x$ to an open set of the model space $E$. Writing $y = \psi_x (x) \in E$, let: \begin{align*} B_{n, x} &= \psi_x^{-1} (B_E(y, r)),\\ W_{n, x} &= \psi_x^{-1} (f_{y,r} (B_E (0, 1))),\\ \end{align*} for some $r > 0$ (which may depend on $n$, $x$) sufficiently small that: \begin{itemize} \item $B_E(y, r)$ lies in the target of the chart $\psi_x$, \item $B_{n,x}$ is contained in $U_n$, \item $B_{n,x}$ is contained in $V_j$ for some $j$. \end{itemize} Note that $x \in W_{n,x}$. For each $n$, choose a finite subcovering of $C_n$ by $W_{n, x_1}, \ldots, W_{n, x_{l_n}}$ and define $\iota \subseteq ℕ \times M$ by: \begin{align*} \iota = \bigcup_n \{ (n, x_1), \ldots, (n, x_{l_n}) \} . \end{align*} Note that $\iota$ is countable and furthermore: \begin{itemize} \item for each $i \in \iota$, there is some $j$ such that $B_i \subseteq V_j$, \item $(B_i)_{i \in \iota}$ is locally-finite (indeed more is true: $B_i$ meets only finitely-many $B_{i'}$ for $i, i' \in \iota$ since $B_{m, x} \cap B_{n, x'} = \emptyset$ if $|n - m| > 2$), \item $(W_i)_{i \in \iota}$ covers $M$. \end{itemize} Given $i = (n, x_j) \in \iota$, the required map $\phi_i : E \to M$ is just: \begin{align*} E \simeq B_E(y_j, r) \simeq B_{n,j} \subseteq M. \end{align*} Since $ι$ is countable, it is in bijection with some $\IT{N}$.
nodes.statement_short: Compact exhaustion argument: cover annuli $C_n$ by finitely many small chart balls inside $U_n$, giving a countable locally finite family.

nodes.statement: Let $f : M → N$ be a continuous map between manifolds. nodes.statement: For every bundle $p : E → B$ and every map $f \co B' → B$, the pull-back bundle $f^*E → B'$ is defined by $f^*E = \{(b', e) ∈ B' × E \;|\; p(e) = f(b')\}$ with the obvious projection to $B'$.
nodes.label: def:pull_back_bundle

nodes.name: Hom bundle
nodes.statement: Let $E → B$ and $F → B$ be two vector bundles over some smooth manifold $B$. The bundle $\Hom(E, F) → B$ is the set of linear maps from $E_b$ to $F_b$ for some $b$ in $B$, with the obvious projection map.
nodes.label: def:hom_bundle

nodes.name: 1-jet space J^1(M, N)
nodes.statement: Let $M$ and $N$ be smooth manifolds. Denote by $p_1$ and $p_2$ the projections of $M × N$ to $M$ and $N$ respectively. The space $J^1(M, N)$ of $1$-jets of maps from $M$ to $N$ is $Hom(p_1^*TM, p_2^*TN)$
nodes.label: def:one_jet_space

nodes.name: notation (m, n, φ) for 1-jets
nodes.statement: We will use notations like $(m, n, φ)$ to denote an element of $J^1(M, N)$, but one should keep in mind that $J^1(M, N)$ is not a product, since $φ$ lives in $\Hom(T_mM, T_nN)$ which depends on $m$ and $n$.

nodes.name: 1-jet of a map
nodes.statement: The $1$-jet of a smooth map $f \co M → N$ is the map from $m$ to $J^1(M, N)$ defined by $j^1f(m) = (m, f(m), T_mf)$.
also_stated_at: Any smooth map $f \co M → N$ gives rise to a section $j^1f$ of $J^1(M, N) → M$ defined by $j^1f(m) = (m, f(m), T_m f)$.
nodes.label: def:one_jet_extension

nodes.name: base map of a section
nodes.statement: The composition of a section $\F \co M → J^1(M, N)$ with the projection onto $N$ will sometimes be denoted by $\bs \F \co M → N$ and called the base map of $\F$.

nodes.name: linear component F(m)_φ
nodes.statement: For any $m$, $\F(m)_φ$ will denote the component of $\F(m)$ living in $\Hom(T_mM, T_{\bs\F(m)}N)$.

nodes.name: properties of 1-jet extension
nodes.statement: For every smooth map $f \co M → N$, \begin{enumerate} \item $j^1f$ is smooth \item $j^1f$ is a section of $J^1(M, N) → M$ \end{enumerate}
assumptions: For every smooth map $f \co M → N$,
conclusions: $j^1f$ is smooth
$j^1f$ is a section of $J^1(M, N) → M$
nodes.label: lem:one_jet_extension_prop

nodes.name: Proof of properties of 1-jet extension
nodes.statement: Points 2 and 3 are obvious by construction. To show that $j^1f$ is smooth, suppose that $M$ is modelled over $E$ with charts $C_x : M \to E$ and coordinate change functions $C_{x,x'}=C_{x'}C_x^{-1} : E \to E$ and similarly let $C'_y$ be charts for $N$. By construction of the 1-jet bundle, we need to check that for each $x_0$ the map $$x\mapsto TC'_{f(x),f(x_0)}\circ T(C'_{f(x)}fC_x^{-1})\circ T_{C_{x_0}(x)}(C_{x_0,x}): M \to L(E,E)$$ is smooth at $x_0$ (we occasionally omit the point where the tangent maps are taken). For $x$ close to $x_0$ the coordinate changes are smooth, so we can write \begin{align*} TC'_{f(x),f(x_0)}\circ T(C'_{f(x)}fC_x^{-1})\circ T(C_{x_0,x}) &= T_{C_{x_0}(x)}(C'_{f(x),f(x_0)}C'_{f(x)}fC_x^{-1}C_{x_0,x})\\ &= T_{C_{x_0}(x)}(C'_{f(x_0)}fC_{x_0}) \end{align*} This is smooth since $C'_{f(x_0)}fC_{x_0}$ is smooth.
nodes.statement_short: Section property is by construction; smoothness by computing in charts, where coordinate changes cancel.

nodes.name: Section property obvious; set up charts
nodes.statement: Points 2 and 3 are obvious by construction. To show that $j^1f$ is smooth, suppose that $M$ is modelled over $E$ with charts $C_x : M \to E$ and coordinate change functions $C_{x,x'}=C_{x'}C_x^{-1} : E \to E$ and similarly let $C'_y$ be charts for $N$.
nodes.statement_short: Section property obvious; set up charts

nodes.statement: By construction of the 1-jet bundle, we need to check that for each $x_0$ the map $$x\mapsto TC'_{f(x),f(x_0)}\circ T(C'_{f(x)}fC_x^{-1})\circ T_{C_{x_0}(x)}(C_{x_0,x}): M \to L(E,E)$$ is smooth at $x_0$ (we occasionally omit the point where the tangent maps are taken).
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to smoothness of a chart expression

nodes.name: Chain rule simplifies the expression
nodes.statement: For $x$ close to $x_0$ the coordinate changes are smooth, so we can write \begin{align*} TC'_{f(x),f(x_0)}\circ T(C'_{f(x)}fC_x^{-1})\circ T(C_{x_0,x}) &= T_{C_{x_0}(x)}(C'_{f(x),f(x_0)}C'_{f(x)}fC_x^{-1}C_{x_0,x})\\ &= T_{C_{x_0}(x)}(C'_{f(x_0)}fC_{x_0}) \end{align*}

nodes.name: The simplified map is smooth
nodes.statement: This is smooth since $C'_{f(x_0)}fC_{x_0}$ is smooth.
nodes.statement_short: The simplified map is smooth

nodes.name: holonomic section
nodes.statement: A section $\F$ of $J^1(M, N) → M$ is called holonomic if it is the $1$--jet of its base map. Equivalently, $\F$ is holonomic if there exists $f \co M → N$ such that $\F = j^1f$, since such a map is necessarily $\bs \F$.
also_stated_at: Such a section is called a \emph{holonomic section} of $J^1(M, N)$.
nodes.label: def:holonomic_section

nodes.name: first order differential relation
nodes.statement: A first order differential relation for maps from $M$ to $N$ is a subset $\Rel$ of $J^1(M, N)$.
nodes.label: def:rel

nodes.name: formal solution
nodes.statement: A formal solution of a differential relation $\Rel ⊂ J^1(M, N)$ is a section of $J^1(M, N) → M$ taking values in $\Rel$.
nodes.label: def:formal_sol

nodes.name: homotopy of formal solutions
nodes.statement: A homotopy of formal solutions of $\Rel$ is a smooth family of sections $\F : ℝ × M → J^1(M, N)$ such that each $m ↦ \F(t, m)$ is a formal solution.
nodes.label: def:htpy_formal_sol

nodes.name: transfer map
nodes.statement: Given manifolds $M$, $X$, $N$ and $Y$ and smooth open embeddings $g : Y → N$ and $h : X → M$ we get a transfer map $ψ_{g, h} : J^1(X, Y) → J^1(M, N)$ defined by \[ ψ_{g, h}(x, y, φ) = (h(x), g(y), T_yg ∘ φ ∘ (T_xh)⁻¹) \] and an operator on sections which sends $\F : M → J^1(M, N)$ to $Ψ_{g, h}\F : X → J^1(X, Y)$ defined when $\bs\F(h(X)) ⊂ g(Y)$ by \[ Ψ_{g, h}\F(x) = (x, g⁻¹ ∘ \bs\F ∘ h(x), (T_{g⁻¹ ∘ \bs\F ∘ h(x)}g)⁻¹ ∘ \F(h(x))_φ ∘ T_xh). \] Given a relation $\Rel ⊂ J^1(M, N)$, the induced relation in $J^1(X, Y)$ is $ψ_{g, h}⁻¹\Rel$.
nodes.statement_short: Open embeddings $g,h$ transport 1-jets to $J^1(M,N)$ and sections back to $J^1(X,Y)$, inducing relations.
nodes.label: def:transfer_map

nodes.name: localization via transfer
nodes.statement: In the situation of the previous definition, given a section $\F : M → J^1(M, N)$: \begin{itemize} \item $Ψ_{g, h}(\F)$ is a smooth section of $J^1(X, Y)$. \item $\F$ is holonomic on $s ⊂ h(X) ∩ \bs\F⁻¹(g(Y))$ if and only if $Ψ_{g, h}(\F)$ is holonomic on $h⁻¹(s)$. \item $\F$ is a formal solution of $\Rel$ on $h(X) ∩ \bs\F⁻¹(g(Y)$ if and only if $Ψ_{g, h}(\F)$ is a formal solution of the induced relation $Ψ_{g, h}⁻¹\Rel$. \end{itemize}
nodes.statement_short: Transfer preserves smoothness, holonomy and being a formal solution of the induced relation.
assumptions: In the situation of the previous definition, given a section $\F : M → J^1(M, N)$:
conclusions: $Ψ_{g, h}(\F)$ is a smooth section of $J^1(X, Y)$.
$\F$ is holonomic on $s ⊂ h(X) ∩ \bs\F⁻¹(g(Y))$ if and only if $Ψ_{g, h}(\F)$ is holonomic on $h⁻¹(s)$.
nodes.label: lem:transfer

nodes.name: Proof of localization via transfer
nodes.statement: The first point is clear by composition. In order to prove the second point while keeping notations under control, we set $f(x) = g⁻¹ ∘ \bs\F ∘ h$. Using this notation $Ψ_{g, h}\F(x) = (x, f(x), (T_{f(x)}g)⁻¹ ∘ \F(h(x))_φ ∘ T_xh)$. We have \begin{align*} T_x f &= T_{\bs\F ∘ h(x)}(g⁻¹) ∘ T_{h(x)}\bs\F ∘ T_x h\\ &= \left(T_{f(x)}g\right)⁻¹ ∘ T_{h(x)}\bs\F ∘ T_x h \end{align*} hence $Ψ_{g, h}\F$ is holonomic at $x$ if and only if $\left(T_{f(x)}g\right)⁻¹ ∘ \F(h(x))_φ ∘ T_xh = \left(T_{f(x)}g\right)⁻¹ ∘ T_{h(x)}\bs\F ∘ T_x h$ and this is equivalent to $\F(h(x))_φ = T_{h(x)}\bs\F$ which is the holonomy condition for $\F$ at $h(x)$. The third point is a direct consequence of the easy formula $ψ_{g, h} ∘ Ψ_{g, h}(\F) = F ∘ h$.
nodes.statement_short: Chain rule computation of $T_xf$ shows holonomy conditions correspond; formal solutions via $ψ∘Ψ(\F)=\F∘h$.

nodes.name: First point; set $f = g⁻¹∘\bs\F∘h$
nodes.statement: The first point is clear by composition. In order to prove the second point while keeping notations under control, we set $f(x) = g⁻¹ ∘ \bs\F ∘ h$.
nodes.statement_short: First point; set $f = g⁻¹∘\bs\F∘h$

nodes.name: Rewrite $Ψ_{g,h}\F$
nodes.statement: Using this notation $Ψ_{g, h}\F(x) = (x, f(x), (T_{f(x)}g)⁻¹ ∘ \F(h(x))_φ ∘ T_xh)$.
nodes.statement_short: Rewrite $Ψ_{g,h}\F$

nodes.name: Chain rule gives holonomy equivalence; third point by a formula
nodes.statement: We have \begin{align*} T_x f &= T_{\bs\F ∘ h(x)}(g⁻¹) ∘ T_{h(x)}\bs\F ∘ T_x h\\ &= \left(T_{f(x)}g\right)⁻¹ ∘ T_{h(x)}\bs\F ∘ T_x h \end{align*} hence $Ψ_{g, h}\F$ is holonomic at $x$ if and only if $\left(T_{f(x)}g\right)⁻¹ ∘ \F(h(x))_φ ∘ T_xh = \left(T_{f(x)}g\right)⁻¹ ∘ T_{h(x)}\bs\F ∘ T_x h$ and this is equivalent to $\F(h(x))_φ = T_{h(x)}\bs\F$ which is the holonomy condition for $\F$ at $h(x)$. The third point is a direct consequence of the easy formula $ψ_{g, h} ∘ Ψ_{g, h}(\F) = F ∘ h$.
nodes.statement_short: Chain rule gives holonomy equivalence; third point by a formula

nodes.name: h-principle and parametric h-principle
nodes.statement: A first order differential relation $\Rel ⊂ J^1(M, N)$ satisfies the $h$-principle if every formal solution of $\Rel$ is homotopic to a holonomic one. It satisfies the parametric $h$-principle if, for every manifold $P$ and every closed set $C$ in $P × M$, every family $\F : P × M → J^1(M, N)$ of formal solutions which are holonomic for $(p, m)$ near $C$ is homotopic to a family of holonomic ones relative to $C$.
nodes.label: def:h-princ

nodes.name: manifolds X, P, Y with parameter space P
nodes.statement: Let $X$, $P$ and $Y$ be manifolds, with $P$ seen a parameter space.

nodes.name: forgetful map Ψ on jets
nodes.statement: Denote by $Ψ$ the map from $J^1(X × P, Y)$ to $J^1(X, Y)$ sending $(x, p, y, ψ)$ to $(x, y, ψ ∘ ι_{x, p})$ where $ι_{x, p} : T_xX → T_xX × T_pP$ sends $v$ to $(v, 0)$.

nodes.name: associated section F bar
nodes.statement: To any family of sections $F_p : x ↦ (f_p(x), φ_{p, x})$ of $J^1(X, Y)$, we associate the section $\bar F$ of $J^1(X × P, Y)$ sending $(x, p)$ to $\bar F(x, p) := (f_p(x), φ_{p, x} ⊕ ∂f/∂p(x, p))$.

nodes.name: parametric trick
nodes.statement: In the above setup, we have: \begin{itemize} \item $\bar F$ is holonomic at $(x, p)$ if and only if $F_p$ is holonomic at $x$. \item $F$ is a family of formal solutions of some $\Rel ⊂ J^1(X, Y)$ if and only if $\bar F$ is a formal solution of $\Rel^P := Ψ^{-1}(\Rel)$. \end{itemize}
assumptions: In the above setup
conclusions: $\bar F$ is holonomic at $(x, p)$ if and only if $F_p$ is holonomic at $x$.
$F$ is a family of formal solutions of some $\Rel ⊂ J^1(X, Y)$ if and only if $\bar F$ is a formal solution of $\Rel^P := Ψ^{-1}(\Rel)$.
nodes.label: lem:param_trick

nodes.name: Proof of parametric trick
nodes.statement: For the first part, the derivative of $\bar F$ is $∂f/∂x(x, p) ⊕ ∂f/∂p(x, p)$, which is equal to $\bar F_φ$ iff $∂f/∂x(x, p) = f_φ$. The second part follows from $Ψ ∘ \bar F(x,p)=F_p(x)$.
nodes.statement_short: Compare derivatives componentwise; use $Ψ∘\bar F = F_p$.

nodes.name: parametricity for free
nodes.statement: Let $\Rel$ be a first order differential relation for maps from $M$ to $N$. If, for every manifold with boundary $P$, $\Rel^P$ satisfies the $h$-principle then $\Rel$ satisfies the parametric $h$-principle. Likewise, the $C^0$-dense and relative $h$-principle for all $\Rel^P$ imply the parametric $C^0$-dense and relative $h$-principle for $\Rel$.
assumptions: Let $\Rel$ be a first order differential relation for maps from $M$ to $N$.
If, for every manifold with boundary $P$, $\Rel^P$ satisfies the $h$-principle
conclusions: then $\Rel$ satisfies the parametric $h$-principle.
Likewise, the $C^0$-dense and relative $h$-principle for all $\Rel^P$ imply the parametric $C^0$-dense and relative $h$-principle for $\Rel$.
nodes.label: lem:param_for_free

nodes.name: Proof of parametricity for free
nodes.statement: By \cref{lem:param_trick} we can turn a formal solution of $\Rel$ into a formal solution of $\Rel^P$, so we get a homotopy to a holonomic formal solution. We can turn this homotopy back to a homotopy of the original formal solution.
nodes.statement_short: Turn families into single formal solutions of $\Rel^P$ via the parametric trick and back.

nodes.name: convention: X, Y manifolds and R a relation in J^1(X, Y)
nodes.statement: In this chapter, $X$ and $Y$ are smooth manifolds and $\Rel$ is a first order differential relation on maps from $X$ to $Y$: $\Rel ⊂ J^1(X, Y)$.

nodes.name: slice R_{σ, λ, v} of a relation
nodes.statement: For any $σ = (x, y, φ)$ in $\Rel$ and any dual pair $(λ, v) ∈ T^*_xX × T_xX$, we set: \[ \Rel_{σ, λ, v} = \Conn_{φ(v)}\left\{w ∈ T_yY \;;\; \big(x,\; y,\; φ + (w - φ(v))⊗λ\big) ∈ \Rel\right\} \] where $\Conn_a A$ is the connected component of $A$ containing $a$.
nodes.section: 3.3 The $h$-principle for open and ample differential relations
nodes.statement_short: The slice is the connected component containing $φ(v)$ of the $w$ such that updating $φ$ along $(λ,v)$ to send $v$ to $w$ stays in $\Rel$.

nodes.name: slices depend only on ker λ and the direction
nodes.statement: One easily checks that $\Rel_{σ, κ^{-1}λ, κv} = κ\Rel_{σ, λ, v}$ hence the above definition only depends on $\ker λ$ and the direction $ℝV$.

conclusions: $\Rel_{σ, κ^{-1}λ, κv} = κ\Rel_{σ, λ, v}$
the above definition only depends on $\ker λ$ and the direction $ℝV$

nodes.name: ample relation
nodes.statement: A relation $\Rel$ is ample if, for every $σ = (x, y, φ)$ in $\Rel$ and every $(λ, v)$, the slice $\Rel_{σ, λ, v}$ is ample in $T_yY$.
nodes.section: 3.3 The $h$-principle for open and ample differential relations
differentia: for every $σ = (x, y, φ)$ in $\Rel$ and every $(λ, v)$, the slice $\Rel_{σ, λ, v}$ is ample in $T_yY$
nodes.label: def:ample_relation

nodes.name: induced relations of ample relations are ample
nodes.statement: Given manifolds $W$, $X$, $Y$ and $Z$ and smooth open embeddings $g : Z → Y$ and $h : W → X$, the relation induced (in the sense of \Cref{def:transfer_map}) in $J^1(W, Z)$ by an ample relation in $J^1(X, Y)$ is ample.
nodes.section: 3.3 The $h$-principle for open and ample differential relations
assumptions: Given manifolds $W$, $X$, $Y$ and $Z$ and smooth open embeddings $g : Z → Y$ and $h : W → X$,
conclusions: the relation induced (in the sense of \Cref{def:transfer_map}) in $J^1(W, Z)$ by an ample relation in $J^1(X, Y)$ is ample.
nodes.label: lem:ample_iff_loc

nodes.name: Proof that induced relations of ample relations are ample
nodes.statement: By definition, the relation induced by $\Rel$ is $ψ_{g, h}⁻¹\Rel$ where $ψ_{g, h}(w, z, φ) = (h(w), g(z), T_zg ∘ φ ∘ (T_wh)⁻¹)$. Fix $σ =(w, z, φ) ∈ ψ_{g, h}⁻¹\Rel$ and a dual pair $(λ, v)$ on $T_wW$. We set $G = T_z g$ and $H = T_w h$. Both those maps are linear isomorphisms. We compute the slice corresponding to $(σ, λ, v)$: \begin{align*} ψ_{g, h}⁻¹\Rel(σ, λ, v) &= \Conn_{φv}\left\{u ∈ T_wW \;\left|\; (w, z, φ + (u - φv)⊗λ) ∈ ψ_{g, h}⁻¹\Rel \right.\right\}\\ &= \Conn_{φv}\left\{u ∈ T_wW \;\left|\; (h(w), g(z), G ∘ (φ + (u - φv)⊗λ)∘ H⁻¹) ∈ \Rel \right.\right\}\\ &= G⁻¹\Rel(ψ_{g, h}σ, λ ∘ H⁻¹, Hv). \end{align*} Hence the slice $ψ_{g, h}⁻¹\Rel(σ, λ, v)$ is the image of a slice of $\Rel$ under a linear isomorphism, hence ample.
nodes.section: 3.3 The $h$-principle for open and ample differential relations
nodes.statement_short: Compute the induced slice as the image of a slice of $\Rel$ under a linear isomorphism.

nodes.name: Unfold the induced relation
nodes.statement: By definition, the relation induced by $\Rel$ is $ψ_{g, h}⁻¹\Rel$ where $ψ_{g, h}(w, z, φ) = (h(w), g(z), T_zg ∘ φ ∘ (T_wh)⁻¹)$.

nodes.name: immersion relation is open and ample
nodes.statement: The relation of immersions of $M$ into $N$ in positive codimension is open and ample.
nodes.section: 3.3 The $h$-principle for open and ample differential relations
assumptions: in positive codimension
conclusions: The relation of immersions of $M$ into $N$ in positive codimension is open and ample.
nodes.label: lem:open_ample_immersion

nodes.name: Proof that the immersion relation is open and ample
nodes.statement: For every $σ = (x, y, φ)$ in the immersion relation $\Rel$, and for every dual pair $(π, v)$, the slice $\Rel(σ, π, v)$ is the set of $w$ which do not belong to the image of $\ker π$ under $φ$. Since $\dim M > \dim N$, this image has codimension at least $2$ in $T_yN$, and \cref{lem:ample_codim_two} concludes.
nodes.section: 3.3 The $h$-principle for open and ample differential relations
nodes.statement_short: Slices are complements of the image of $\ker π$, of codimension at least two.

nodes.name: Gromov's h-principle for open and ample relations
nodes.statement: For any manifolds $X$ and $Y$, any relation $\Rel ⊂ J^1(X, Y)$ that is open and ample satisfies the full $h$-principle (relative, parametric and $C^0$-dense).

nodes.name: ampleness of the parametric relation
nodes.statement: If $\Rel$ is ample then, for any parameter space $P$, $\Rel^P$ is also ample.

assumptions: If $\Rel$ is ample
conclusions: then, for any parameter space $P$, $\Rel^P$ is also ample.

nodes.name: Proof of ampleness of the parametric relation
nodes.statement: We fix $σ = (x, y, ψ)$ in $\Rel^P$. For any $λ = (λ_X, λ_P) ∈ T^*_xX × T^*_pP$ and $v = (v_X, v_P) ∈ T_xX × T_pP$ such that $λ(v) = 1$, we need to prove that $\Conv\Rel^P_{σ, λ, v} = T_yY$. Unfolding the definitions gives: \[ \Rel^P_{σ, λ, v} = \Conn_{φ(v)}\left\{w ∈ T_yY \;;\; \big(x,\; y,\; ψ ∘ ι_{x, p} + (w - ψ(v))⊗λ_X\big) ∈ \Rel\right\}. \] A degenerate but easy case is when $λ_X = 0$. Then the condition on $w$ becomes $ψ ∘ ι_{x, p} ∈ \Rel$, which is true by definition of $\Rel^P$, so $\Rel^P_{σ, λ, v} = T_yY$. We now assume $λ_X$ is not zero and choose $u ∈ T_xX$ such that $λ_X(u) = 1$. We then have $\Rel^P_{σ, λ, v} = \Rel_{Ψσ, λ_X, u} + ψ(v) - ψ∘ι_{x, p}(u)$. Because $\Rel$ is ample and taking convex hull commutes with translation, we get that $\Conv\Rel^P_{σ, λ, v} = T_yY$.

nodes.name: Proof of Gromov's h-principle for open and ample relations
nodes.statement: Lemmas~\ref{lem:param_for_free} and~\ref{lem:ample_parameter} prove we can assume there are no parameters. So we start with a single formal solution $F₀$ of $\Rel$, which is holonomic near some closed subset $A ⊂ X$. We also fix a positive continuous function $δ$ on $X$ and we want to build a homotopy of formal solutions starting at $F₀$ relative to $A$ with base map staying at distance at most $δ$ from the base map of $F₀$ and ending at a holonomic solution. We apply \cref{lem:ex_localisation} to get some localisation data $(φ \co \IT{N} × E → \set{X}, ψ \co ι × E' → \set{Y}, j)$ for $\bs F₀ : X → Y$. \Cref{lem:localisation_stability} then provides a continuous function $ε : X → ℝ_{> 0}$ such that every function $g$ with $d(\bs F₀, g) < ε$ sends each $φ_i(E)$ into $ψ_{j(i)}(E')$. We denote by $τ$ the positive continuous function $\min(δ, ε)$. We then use the inductive construction of homotopies provided by \Cref{lem:inductive_htpy_construction} starting with $F₀$ and using the following local predicates. On maps $F$ from $X$ to $J¹(X, Y)$ we use the background predicate $P₀$ asserting that $F$ is a smooth section of $J¹(X, Y) → X$ that takes values in $R$, coincides with $F₀$ near $A$ and satisfies $d(\bs F, \bs F₀) < τ$. The background predicate for maps from $ℝ × X$ to $J¹(X, Y)$ is simply smoothness and the target local predicate $P₁$ on maps from $X$ to $J¹(X, Y)$ is being holonomic. We use the family of sets $U \co i ↦ φ_i(E)$ and $K \co i ↦ φ_i(\bar{B}_E)$. In order to check the induction assumption from \Cref{lem:inductive_htpy_construction}, we fix some $i$ in $\IT{N}$, and some formal solution $F$ which coincides with $F₀$ near $A$ and such that $d(\bs F₀, \bs F) < τ$. We assume that $F$ is holonomic near $\bigcup_{j < i} K_j$. We need to build a smooth homotopy of formal solutions starting at $F$ which coincide with $F₀$ near $A$, coincide with $F$ outside $U_i$, have base map at distance less than $τ$ from $\bs F₀$ and end at a formal solution which is holonomic near $\bigcup_{j ≤ i} K_j$. In addition this homotopy must be time-independent for time near $(-∞, 0]$ and $[1, +∞)$. Of course this homotopy comes from the local $h$-principle we proved in \Cref{lem:h_principle_open_ample_loc}. The first key observation allowing to apply that lemma is that $d(\bs F, \bs F₀) < τ ≤ ε$ hence $\bs F$ sends sends $φ_i(E)$ into $ψ_{j(i)}(E')$. \Cref{def:transfer_map} then turns $F$ into a section $\F$ of $J¹(E, E')$. According to \Cref{lem:transfer}, $\F$ is a formal solution of the relation $\Rel_i$ induced by $\Rel$ in $J¹(E, E')$ via $φ_i$ and $ψ_{j(i)}$, $\F$ is relative to $φ_i⁻¹(A)$ and $\F$ is holonomic near $φ_i⁻¹(A ∪ \bigcup_{j < i} φ_j(\bar B_E))$. The homotopy $H$ will be constructed by updating $F$ using some homotopy $\HH$ of sections of $J¹(E, E')$ with support in the closed ball $2B_E$ and time independent for $t$ near $(-∞, 0] ∪ [1, +∞)$ (here by support we mean the closure of the set of points where $\HH_t$ differs from $\F$). In order to ensure $d(\bs F₀, \bs H_t) < τ$ for all $t$, it suffices to ensure that, for each $x ∈ φ_i(2\bar{B}_E)$ and $t ∈ [0, 1]$, $d(\bs H_t(x), \bs F(x)) < τ(x) - d(\bs F(x), \bs F₀(x))$. The latter will hold as soon as, for all $e$ and $t$, $‖\bs \HH_t(e) - \bs \F(e)‖ < η$ for some positive $η$ given by \Cref{lem:dist_updating} (applied to $P = ℝ$, $M$ and $N$).

nodes.name: Proof that the local immersion relation is open
nodes.statement: The main task is to fix $x_0 \notin B$ and $\varphi_0 \in L(E, E)$ which is injective on $x_0^\perp$ and prove that, for every $x$ close to $x_0$ and $\varphi$ close to $\varphi_0$, $\varphi$ is injective on $x^\perp$. This is a typical situation where geometric intuition makes it feel like there is nothing to prove. One difficulty is that the subspace $x^\perp$ moves with $x$. We reduce to a fixed subspace by considering the restriction to $x_0^\perp$ of the orthogonal projection onto $x^\perp$. One can check this is an isomorphism as long as $x$ is not perpendicular to $x_0$. More precisely, we consider $f \co J^1(E, E) \to ℝ \times L(x_0^\perp, E)$ which sends $(x, y, \varphi)$ to $(\langle x_0, x\rangle, \varphi \circ \pr_{x^\perp} \circ j_0)$ where $j_0$ is the inclusion of $x_0^\perp$ into $E$. The set $U$ of injective linear maps is open in $L(x_0^\perp, E)$ and the map $f$ is continuous hence the preimage of $\{0\}^c \times U$ is open. This is good enough for us because injectivity of $\varphi \circ \pr_{x^\perp} \circ j_0$ implies injectivity of $\varphi$ on the image of $\pr_{x^\perp} \circ j_0$ which is $x^\perp$ whenever $\langle x_0, x\rangle \neq 0$.

nodes.name: Proof that the local immersion relation is ample
nodes.statement: The core fact here is that if one fixes vector spaces $F$ and $F'$, a dual pair $(\pi, v)$ on $F$ and an injective linear map $\varphi \co F \to F'$ then the updated map $\Upd{p}{\varphi}{w}$ is injective if and only if $w$ is not in $\varphi(\ker\pi)$. First we assume $\Upd{p}{\varphi}{\varphi(u)}$ is injective for some $u$ in $\varphi(\ker\pi)$ and derive a contradiction. We have $\Upd{p}{\varphi}{\varphi(u)}v = \varphi(u)$ by the general definition of updating and also $\Upd{p}{\varphi}{\varphi(u)}u = \varphi(u)$ since $u$ is in $\ker \pi$. Hence injectivity of $\varphi$ ensure $u = v$, which is absurd since $\pi(u) = 0$ and $\pi(v) = 1$. Conversely assume $w$ is not in $\varphi(\ker\pi)$ and let us prove $\Upd{p}{\varphi}{w}$ is injective. Assume $x$ is in the kernel of $\Upd{p}{\varphi}{w}$. Decompose $x = u + tv$ with $u \in \ker\pi$ and $t$ a real number. We have $\Upd{p}{\varphi}{w}(x) = \varphi(u) + tw$. Hence our assumption on $x$ implies $t$ vanishes otherwise we would have $w = -t⁻¹\varphi(u)$ contradicting that $w$ isn't in $\varphi(\ker\pi)$. This vanishing and the assumption on $x$ then imply $\varphi(u) = 0$. Since $\varphi$ is injective we conclude that $u = 0$ and finally $x = 0$. We now turn to $\Rel$. It suffices to prove that for every $\sigma = (x, y, \varphi) \in \Rel$ and every dual pair $p = (\pi, v)$ on $E$, the slice $\Rel(\sigma, p)$ is ample. If $x$ is in $B$ then $\Rel(\sigma, p)$ is the whole $E$ which is obviously ample. So we assume $x$ is not in $B$. Since $\sigma$ is in $\Rel$, $\varphi$ is injective on $x^\perp$. The slice is the set of $w$ such that $\Upd{p}{\varphi}{w}$ is injective on $x^\perp$. Assume first $\ker\pi = x^\perp$. Then $\Upd{p}{\varphi}{w}$ coincides with $\varphi$ on $x^\perp$ hence the slice is the whole $E$. Assume now that $\ker\pi \neq x^\perp$. The slice is not very easy to picture in this case. But one should remember that, up to affine isomorphism, the slice depends only on $\ker \pi$. More specifically, if we keep $\pi$ but change $v$ then the slice is simply translated in $E$. Here we replace $v$ by the projection on $x^\perp$ of the vector dual to $\pi$ rescaled to keep the property $\pi(v) = 1$. What has been gained is that we now have $v \in x^\perp$ and $x^\perp = (x^\perp \cap \ker \pi) \oplus ℝ v$. Since $\varphi$ is injective on $x^\perp$, $\varphi(x^\perp \cap \ker \pi)$ is a hyperplane in $x^\perp$ and $\Upd{p}{\varphi}{w}$ is injective on $x^\perp$ if and only if $w$ is in the complement of $\varphi(x^\perp \cap \ker \pi)$ according to the core fact above. Since it is an hyperplane in $x^\perp$, it has codimension at least $2$ in $E$ hence its complement is ample.

nodes.name: germ and local predicate

nodes.name: Proof of inductive construction of homotopies
nodes.statement: Carefully checking all details is a bit technical but the strategy is as follows. We fix an increasing sequence $T \co \IT{N} → [0, 1)$ starting at $0$, say $i ↦ 1 - 1/2^i$. We want to build a sequence of homotopies $F_i \co ℝ × X → Y$ where each $F_i$ is time-independent on $[T_i, + ∞) × X$ and, assuming $i$ isn't maximal, $F_{S(i)}$ is built from $F_i$ by applying the induction assumption to $F_i(T_i, \cdot)$ and rescaling the obtained homotopy by the affine map sending $[0, 1]$ to $[T_i, T_{S(i)}]$. Hence we want to apply \Cref{lem:inductive_construction} with source space $\hat{X} = ℝ × X$. We use as the background local predicate $\hat{P}₀$ at $(t, x)$ the constraint on a function $F$ that $F(t, \cdot)$ satisfies $P₀$ at $x$ and $P₀'$ at $(t, x)$ and if $t = 0$ then $F(t, x) = f₀(x)$. As the target family of local predicates $\hat{P}₁$ we use for every $i ∈ \IT{N}$ the constraint on $F$ at $(t, x)$ that if $t = 1$ and $x$ is near $K_i$ then $F(t, \cdot)$ should satisfy $P₂$ at $x$. As the auxiliary family of predicates $\hat{P₂}$ at index $i$ we use the constraint of being time-independent on $[T_i, + ∞) × X$. In order to explain how the induction assumption of the current lemma implies the induction assumption of \Cref{lem:inductive_construction}, we fix $i ∈ \IT{N}$ and a map $F \co ℝ × X → Y$ that satisfies $\hat{P}₀$, is time-independent on $[T_i, + ∞) × X$ and satisfies $\hat{P}₁^j$ for all $j < i$. By this last requirement and the time independence property, we get that $F(T_i, \cdot)$ satisfies $P₁$ near $\bigcup_{j < i} K_j$. Our induction assumption applied to $F(T_i, \cdot)$ then gives $F' \co ℝ × X → Y$ such that \begin{itemize} \item for all $t$, $F'(t, \cdot)$ satisfies $P₀$ \item $F'$ satisfies $P₀'$ \item $F'(1, \cdot)$ satisfies $P₁$ on $\bigcup_{j ≤ i} K_j$ \item $F'(t, x) = f(x)$ whenever $x$ is not in $U_i$ or $t$ is near $(-∞, 0]$ \item $F'(t, x) = F(1, x)$ whenever $t$ is near $[1, +∞)$. \end{itemize} As the new map required by the inductive assumption of \Cref{lem:inductive_construction}, we pick \[ F'' \co (t, x) ↦ \begin{cases} F(t, x) \text{ if $t ≤ T_i$}\\ F'\left((t - T_i)/(T_{S(i)} - T_i), x\right) \text{ if $t > T_i$} \end{cases} \] Fully checking that $F''$ is suitable is fairly technical but mostly straightforward. Care is required in particular to check that $F''$ coincides with $F$ near $(T_i, x)$ for every $x$. Our induction assumption applied to $F(T_i, \cdot)$ then gives $F' \co ℝ × X → Y$ such that \begin{itemize}

nodes.name: Background predicate
nodes.statement: for all $t$, $F'(t, \cdot)$ satisfies $P₀$
nodes.statement_short: Background predicate

nodes.statement: $F'$ satisfies $P₀'$

nodes.statement: $F'(t, x) = f(x)$ whenever $x$ is not in $U_i$ or $t$ is near $(-∞, 0]$
nodes.statement_short: Unchanged outside $U_i$ and near time 0

nodes.name: Constant near time 1
nodes.statement: $F'(t, x) = F(1, x)$ whenever $t$ is near $[1, +∞)$. \end{itemize}

nodes.name: Concatenate to define $F''$
nodes.statement: As the new map required by the inductive assumption of \Cref{lem:inductive_construction}, we pick \[ F'' \co (t, x) ↦ \begin{cases} F(t, x) \text{ if $t ≤ T_i$}\\ F'\left((t - T_i)/(T_{S(i)} - T_i), x\right) \text{ if $t > T_i$} \end{cases} \]
nodes.statement_short: Concatenate to define $F''$

nodes.name: Verify $F''$ using time independence
nodes.statement: Fully checking that $F''$ is suitable is fairly technical but mostly straightforward. Care is required in particular to check that $F''$ coincides with $F$ near $(T_i, x)$ for every $x$. This uses both the fact that $F$ is time-independent on $[T_i, + ∞) × X$ and that $F'$ is time-independent near $(-∞, 0] × X$ hence in particular near $(0, x)$.
nodes.statement_short: Verify $F''$ using time independence

nodes.name: existence of locally finite subcover of local predicate
nodes.statement: Let $X$ be a metrizable locally compact second countable topological space. Let $C$ be a closed subset in $X$. Let $P$ be a non-decreasing predicate on subsets of $X$ (meaning that if $U ⊂ V$ and $V$ satisfies $P$ then so does $U$). Assume the empty set satisfies $P$ and every point in $C$ has a neighborhood in $X$ satisfying $P$.
